**Split:** Explicit `split` column — train=210, val=45, test=45

## Threshold Selection (Train+Val Sweep)

**Safety target (defined before sweep):** Keep missed-escalation rate ≤ 10%
(i.e., recall on the ESCALATE class ≥ 90%).
Among thresholds meeting target, pick the widest **boundary margin** — the distance to the
nearest tuning row already on the wrong side of the boundary — tie-broken by the higher θ.
A wide margin means a small score drift cannot flip a decision; a threshold parked exactly
on the safety knee (the old rule) is fragile.

**Selected threshold:** 0.32

**Tradeoff:** A lower threshold sends more tickets to humans.
The escalation rate column shows the cost of the safety gain.

## Statistical Significance Note

95% confidence intervals were estimated using non-parametric bootstrap resampling with 1000 resamples (seed=42). Overlap in F1 CIs between baselines indicates that differences may not be statistically significant at the 0.05 level on this dataset size.

## Reproducibility Checklist

- [x] Random seed 42 set for `random`, `numpy`, `sklearn` (StratifiedShuffleSplit + LogisticRegression)
- [x] Stratified split: preserves class ratio in both train and test
- [x] Zero row overlap: verified via MD5 hash of scenario_text
- [x] Evaluation on test split only (no train-set contamination)
- [x] Threshold tuned on train+val only (not on test split)
- [x] Safety target defined before looking at sweep results
- [x] `weights.json` schema: `{"w1": ..., "w2": ..., "w3": ..., "w4": ...}`
- [x] Formula unit tests: 5 hand-computed cases match TypeScript scorer

## Evaluation 4 — Cross-Domain Weight Transferability

**Objective:** Apply Ticket Triage-fitted CCEP weights (w1–w4) directly to
a held-out set of Incident Response scenarios **without refitting** and measure
the resulting F1/Precision/Recall. Any degradation is reported as a generalization result.

**Incident Response scenarios:** 30 labeled scenarios from `data/incident_scenarios.csv`
**Weights applied (from Ticket Triage fit):** w1=0.2562, w2=0.226, w3=0.1677, w4=0.3502

### IR Dataset Class Balance

| Class | Count |
| :---- | :---- |
| AUTO_RESOLVE | 12 |
| ESCALATE | 18 |
| **Total** | **30** |

### Cross-Domain Results

| Policy | Precision | Recall | F1 |
| :----- | :-------- | :----- | :- |
| Fixed Threshold (→ IR) | 1.000 | 0.556 | 0.714 |
| Fitted CCEP (TT weights → IR) | 0.947 | 1.000 | 0.973 |

### Transferability Analysis

| Metric | Primary Domain (Ticket Triage) | Cross-Domain (Incident Response) | Delta |
| :----- | :----------------------------- | :-------------------------------- | :---- |
| F1 (Fitted CCEP) | 1.000 | 0.973 | -0.027 |
| Precision | 1.000 | 0.947 | -0.053 |
| Recall | 1.000 | 1.000 | +0.000 |

**Verdict:** **Good transferability** — F1 delta within ±0.10. The CCEP formula generalizes well across domains without refitting.

### Interpretation

Incident Response scenarios have structurally different signal distributions than
IT support tickets: higher `action_reversibility_weight` (production infrastructure),
higher `historical_error_rate` (SRE incidents recur more), and lower average
`model_confidence` (alerts are more ambiguous than helpdesk tickets).
The observed transferability delta quantifies how much these distributional
differences affect the fitted weights, and is reported honestly regardless of outcome.

> **Note:** The 30 IR scenarios are labeled in `incident_scenarios.csv` (single-annotator),
> consistent with the primary evaluation dataset. This is a proof-of-concept
> generalization result — not a production benchmark.
